title: PRE 15 — Test
src: Class II Composite Restoration & Curing Lights

mcqs.q: In the two-step etch-and-rinse Class II procedure, the FIRST step is:
mcqs.explain: The sequence begins with shade selection, then rubber-dam isolation, preparation, matrix/wedge, etch, bond, incremental composite and finishing.

mcqs.q: Isolation of the operating site for a Class II composite is best achieved with:
mcqs.explain: Rubber-dam isolation keeps the field dry and clean, which is essential for a reliable bond.

mcqs.q: Why is proper matrix placement one of the MOST important steps for posterior composites?
opts: Posterior composites depend almost totally on the matrix for the proximal contact
Composite is condensed to form the contact
mcqs.explain: Unlike amalgam (which is condensed to develop contact), posterior composites rely almost entirely on the matrix contour/position for the proximal contact.

mcqs.q: For larger posterior composites, which matrix is preferable?
mcqs.explain: Pre-contoured sectional metallic matrices are preferred; clear polyester strips cannot be contoured and resist condensation poorly.

mcqs.q: The bitine (separating) ring of a sectional system serves to:
opts: Stabilise the band and provide additional tooth separation
mcqs.explain: The bitine ring stabilises the matrix band and provides additional tooth separation, helping establish a proper contact.

mcqs.q: The matrix material should extend at least how far beyond the gingival margin?
opts: It should stop short of the margin
mcqs.explain: Regardless of the system, the matrix should extend at least 1 mm beyond the gingival margin and to the marginal-ridge level occlusally.

mcqs.q: Clear polyester (mylar) matrices are NOT recommended for large posterior composites because they:
opts: Cannot be contoured and resist condensation poorly
mcqs.explain: Clear polyester matrices cannot be contoured and provide inadequate resistance to condensation of viscous composite in large posterior preparations.

mcqs.q: For a posterior restoration the wedge is placed:
opts: From the larger to the smaller embrasure, typically from the lingual, just apical to the gingival margin
mcqs.explain: The wedge is inserted from the larger (usually lingual) embrasure, just apical to the gingival margin, to stabilise the band and prevent overhang.

mcqs.q: In wet (moist) bonding, the etched dentin is kept slightly moist to:
opts: Keep the collagen network expanded for resin infiltration
mcqs.explain: Slight moisture keeps the demineralised collagen network expanded so the adhesive resin can infiltrate it (preventing collapse seen with over-drying).

mcqs.q: After applying the adhesive, it is light-cured for about:
mcqs.explain: The adhesive is polymerised with light curing for about 20 seconds.

mcqs.q: The FIRST composite increment should be placed:
opts: Along the gingival floor of the proximal box, < 2 mm thick
As one bulk fill of 6 mm
mcqs.explain: The first (critical) increment goes along the gingival floor of the box, < 2 mm thick, establishing the gingival seal.

mcqs.q: Why is the first (gingival) increment the most critical?
opts: It is farthest from the light and establishes the gingival seal
It is closest to the light
mcqs.explain: The gingival increment is farthest from the curing light and is critical for a proper gingival seal, so it is kept thin and cured well.

mcqs.q: Each composite increment should generally be no thicker than:
mcqs.explain: Increments are kept to ≤ 2 mm so the curing light can adequately polymerise the full depth.

mcqs.q: Which curing light is MOST commonly used today?
mcqs.explain: LED curing lights are now the most common — efficient and producing little heat.

mcqs.q: The QTH curing light is a:
mcqs.explain: QTH = quartz-tungsten-halogen, an older broad-spectrum light source that generates more heat than LEDs.

mcqs.q: A plasma-arc curing (PAC) light is characterised by:
opts: Very high intensity and fast curing
Being a type of laser scalpel
mcqs.explain: Plasma-arc lights deliver very high intensity, allowing fast curing.

mcqs.q: After curing, the Class II composite is:
opts: Finished and polished (burs/discs) to refine contour, occlusion and smoothness
mcqs.explain: Finishing and polishing with burs/discs refine the contour, occlusion and surface smoothness of the restoration.

mcqs.q: The second increment is typically placed against the:
opts: Lingual (or facial) wall to restore about two-thirds of the box
mcqs.explain: After the gingival increment, a second increment is placed against the lingual (or facial) wall to restore about two-thirds of the box.

mcqs.q: The final increment of the proximal box develops the:
mcqs.explain: The final increment completes the proximal box and develops the marginal ridge contour and contact.

mcqs.q: Before placing composite, the Tofflemire band must be:
opts: In absolute contact with the adjacent contact area
Held away from the adjacent tooth
Cut shorter than the cervical margin
mcqs.explain: The band must be in absolute contact with the adjacent contact area and tall enough to reach below the cervical margin and beyond the marginal ridge.

mcqs.q: The completed restorations shown are:
mcqs.explain: The image shows finished posterior Class II composite restorations with restored contour and contacts.

mcqs.q: Compared with amalgam, posterior composite proximal contact is established mainly by:
mcqs.explain: Amalgam is condensed to develop a contact, but composite cannot be condensed, so the contact depends on matrix contour and position.

saqs.q: List the steps of a two-step etch-and-rinse Class II composite.
saqs.a: Shade → rubber dam → prep → matrix/wedge → etch & wash → adhesive + cure → incremental composite + cure → finish/polish.

saqs.q: Why does posterior composite contact depend on the matrix?
saqs.a: Composite cannot be condensed like amalgam, so the contact depends on the contour and position of the matrix.

saqs.q: What are the advantages of a sectional matrix with a bitine ring?
saqs.a: The ring stabilises the band and provides tooth separation for a strong proximal contact; the band extends ≥1 mm beyond the gingival margin.

saqs.q: Describe the first composite increment and its curing.
saqs.a: Placed along the gingival floor of the box, < 2 mm thick (the critical gingival seal); cured for 20 seconds.

saqs.q: Why are increments limited to ≤ 2 mm?
saqs.a: So the curing light can adequately polymerise the full depth (and reduce shrinkage stress).

saqs.q: Name the types of curing light and the most common one.
saqs.a: QTH (halogen), LED, plasma arc (PAC), laser; LED is the most common today.

saqs.q: What is the purpose of wet (moist) bonding?
saqs.a: Keeping dentin slightly moist keeps the collagen network expanded for proper resin infiltration (avoids collapse from over-drying).
